item.description: Paste your list of people, or type them in. One button shows who to chase today and why, which rows need a date first, and who can wait. Free, no sign-up, nothing leaves your browser.

item.title: Guide: Staying in touch with old leads: what to say after months of silence
item.description: Staying in touch with old leads after months of silence works when you ask for less, not more. Write one line about what they wanted, and give them a way to answer with a number or a single word, including a way to say stop. Try twice, a month apart, then set the lead aside with a date and leave it alone.

item.title: Skill: Reply to a bad guest review without making it worse
item.description: A guest review in, a true public reply, a private message and a to-do list.

item.title: Guide: Recruiter follow up after submitting a candidate: chasing client feedback
item.description: For a recruiter follow up after submitting a candidate, chasing client feedback starts at the submission: ask for a review date and write it down. Chase on that date, not before. Ask for a clear answer: interview, no, or need more from you. If you have no date, chase after three working days, then again, then ask for a straight no.

item.title: Skill: Prepare for a first call from the prospect's website
item.description: A prospect's website in, a one-page brief and questions to ask.

item.title: Guide: Keeping "not now" clients warm without pestering them
item.description: Keeping "not now" clients warm without pestering them starts when they say it: write down why and the date they gave. Contact them on that date, not before. Each message gives them something true, such as a market fact from your desk, and asks one question about the plan. Without a date, about every four to six weeks.

item.title: Guide: How to keep in touch with candidates you did not place
item.description: To keep in touch with candidates you did not place, keep only the people you would call again and write down why while you are on the call. Message them about once a quarter, and at once when a role opens that fits them. Anyone who does not answer two check-ins comes off the list.

item.title: Guide: How to follow up with past clients without being salesy
item.description: To follow up with past clients without being salesy, give every message a reason that is about them: their house, the day they got the keys, something they told you. Never ask whether they are ready to move. Write one or two lines they can answer in a word or ignore, and do it about every three months.

item.title: Guide: How to follow up with a prospect who said they need to think about it
item.description: When a prospect says they need to think about it, ask what they are weighing before you end the call. Send a short recap the same day with the next step in it. Chase once, three or four working days later, with a question they can answer in a word. Then send a last note and put a date in your list.

item.title: Guide: How to follow up with a lead who says call me next month
item.description: When a lead says call me next month, ask for a date before you hang up: which week, and which day suits? Send a one-line note the same day with the date in it. Put the date in your list, so the call is a task and not a memory. Send at most one useful thing in between, and call when you said you would.

item.title: Guide: How to follow up on a quote with no reply
item.description: To follow up on a quote with no reply, ask two working days after you send it whether it arrived and made sense. Five working days later add one new fact and ask one question. Then send a message that closes it. Put the next date in the quote itself so that chasing is expected.

item.title: Guide: How many times to follow up with a client, and when to stop
item.description: There is no magic number of times to follow up with a client. Use a count for the situation. A new enquiry or a quote gets up to three chases, about a working week apart. A client who said later gets one message on the date they gave. A past client gets one about every three months. After the count, stop and park them with a date.

item.title: Guide: Following up with a candidate who went quiet: what to say
item.description: Following up with a candidate who went quiet starts with checking that you are not the one who owes them an update. Then write a short message that gives them an easy way to answer: still interested, not now, or taken another job. Use the channel they use. Two tries, three working days apart, then close it politely.

item.description: Past clients, valuations and old leads: short answers and messages to copy.

item.title: Skill: Follow-up email and CRM note from your call notes

item.title: Guide: Follow up after a valuation or viewing with no reply: what to send
item.description: To follow up after a valuation or viewing with no reply, send a recap the same day with the next step in it. Two working days later send one useful thing. After a week ask one question they can answer in a word, such as what would decide it. Close politely at two weeks and put a date in your diary to try once more.

item.title: Skill: Follow up a lead that went quiet
item.description: A stalled lead's history in, four follow-ups with falling pressure.

item.title: Guide: Estate agent lead follow-up schedule: what to send and when
item.description: An estate agent lead follow-up schedule can be four touches in two weeks: a reply the same day, one useful fact on day 2, one easy question on day 7 and a polite close on day 14. Then park the lead with a date. It runs from a sheet. Each touch says one thing the lead can answer in a word.

item.title: Guide: A simple follow-up system without a CRM
item.description: A simple follow-up system without a CRM is one sheet with four columns: who, last touch, next action, and the date of the next action. Every row must have a date. Each morning, filter for today and earlier, and work down the list for ten minutes. A sheet is enough while you have about twenty live opportunities.

item.title: Skill: Write a cold email from a prospect's website
item.description: A prospect's website in, three emails built on what is on their site.

item.title: Guide: Words for holiday let and rental hosts
item.description: Free replies to guest reviews, messages to guests, house rules, a house manual, sign wording and listing descriptions for rental hosts. Copy them, fill in the gaps.

item.title: Tool: UK late payment interest calculator: statutory rate 11.75% (checked 5 October 2026)
item.description: This UK late payment interest calculator shows what you can charge on an overdue invoice: statutory interest of 8% plus the Bank of England base rate, and a fixed sum on top. Enter the amount and the due date. Every step is shown.

item.title: Guide: Two weeks notice for a retail or hourly job: 14 emails
item.description: In a retail or hourly job, give notice by naming your last shift, not just a date. Say you will work every shift you are rostered until then. Tell your manager in person or by phone first if you can, then send the message so there is a record. In the UK you must give at least a week's notice if you have been in the job more than a month (GOV.UK, read 5 October 2026). Your contract may say more.

item.title: Guide: Two weeks notice email: four you can copy
item.description: A two weeks notice email says you are resigning, gives your last day, offers to help with the handover, and says thank you. A few lines are enough. Do not explain or complain.

item.title: Guide: The words for managing people
item.description: Review phrases, one-to-one questions and opening lines for hard talks. One kit is free.

item.title: Guide: Statement of account email to a customer: 10 examples
item.description: A statement of account lists the invoices you have sent, what has been paid and what is still owed. Send it with a short email: the total due, which items are overdue and how to pay. Use it when a customer has more than one open invoice.

item.title: Guide: Shipment delay email to a customer: four you can copy
item.description: A shipment delay email to a customer should tell them early, say what happened in one fact, give a new date if you have one, and offer a way out. Do not wait for them to ask.

item.title: Guide: Self evaluation examples for work: 12 answers you can adapt, by question (2026)
item.description: A good self evaluation for work gives real examples with dates or numbers, says what was hard, and ends with a goal. The six answers below show how to adapt each part, with gaps for your own facts.

item.title: Guide: Second follow up email after no response: 12 examples
item.description: Wait four to seven days after the first follow-up. Write something new in it: a fact, a question or a smaller ask. Keep it under 60 words. If you still hear nothing after the third message, send a closing note and stop.

item.title: Guide: Scope of work template for freelancers: 13 to copy (Word)
item.description: A scope of work lists what you will deliver, what you will not, what you need from the client, when each part is due and when you are paid. One page is enough. Freelancers can copy one of these Word scopes and point to it when a client asks for "one more thing". It is not a contract, and this is not legal advice.

item.title: Guide: Sales follow up email template after a quote or meeting: 10 to copy (2026)
item.description: A sales follow-up email should refer to something real: a quote, an enquiry, a call or something they said. Name it, ask one question, and make the next step clear.

item.title: Guide: Sales emails you can copy
item.description: Follow-ups, first emails, subject lines and last notes. Copy them, no purchase.

item.title: Guide: Sales breakup email: 9 you can copy, by situation (2026)
item.description: Tell them you will stop writing, make it easy to say no or to reply later, and leave it there. No guilt, no tricks.

item.title: Guide: Return policy template for an online store: four parts to copy
item.description: Say how long buyers have, how to start a return, who pays the postage and when the refund arrives. Keep it the same everywhere it appears in your store.
